predictions.title: ML registry servers log a second max-severity deserialization RCE by Q1 2027
predictions.body: A second named open-source ML data/metadata-plane project will receive a maximum-severity (CVSS >= 9.0) advisory for an unsafe-deserialization remote-code-execution flaw reachable over its network service before any authorization check, by Q1 2027. The class is feature stores, model and artifact registries, metadata/lineage servers, and serialized-transform endpoints — the plumbing that sits behind production inference, not the model or inference engine itself. The structural read from the June 24 Feast advisory (CVE-2026-56121, CVSS 9.3) is that this layer is a soft target by construction: it ingests serialized transformation logic (dill/pickle, joblib, cloudpickle, or equivalent) over gRPC/HTTP/queue surfaces and hands it to a deserializer that executes attacker-controlled __reduce__ payloads as the service account, with no credential required. The same primitive recurs wherever ML infra trusts serialized objects on the wire. The falsifiable core is a NAMED, distinct project (not Feast, and not a re-score or backport of CVE-2026-56121) with its own CVE/GHSA assigned at CVSS >= 9.0 whose root cause is unsafe deserialization of a network-supplied object on an ML registry/feature-store/metadata endpoint. What does NOT count: a non-ML serialization CVE, a sub-9.0 advisory, a hardening commit or proactive 'we removed pickle' changelog with no assigned CVE, or a prompt-injection / model-file (e.g. unsafe model-format) finding. This is the data-and-metadata-plane mirror of the standing malicious-ML-tooling thesis: until deserialization on these endpoints is auth-gated, sandboxed, or replaced with a safe format by default, the answer is the same zero-trust attestation posture, and the recurrence is the evidence the class is real rather than a one-off.

reasoning.because: Feast's June 24 CVE-2026-56121 (CVSS 9.3) is unauth dill.loads RCE on the registry gRPC endpoint
reasoning.given: Feature stores, registries, and metadata servers deserialize network-supplied objects pre-auth
reasoning.so_that: the same unsafe-deserialization RCE primitive recurs in a second named ML data/metadata-plane project
reasoning.landing: Second distinct ML-registry deserialization RCE at CVSS >= 9.0 by Q1 2027
reasoning.plain_language: An AI tool that stores data was hackable because it trusted code sent to it. Soon another similar tool will be caught the same way.

predictions.summary: Feast's June 24 CVE-2026-56121 (CVSS 9.3) was an unauthenticated deserialization RCE on its feature-store registry endpoint. Because ML registries and metadata servers decode serialized objects from the network pre-auth, expect a second named project to log a similar 9.0+ RCE advisory by Q1 2027.

predictions.title: Security vendor ships ML deserialization scanning as a named tier by Q1 2027
predictions.body: By Q1 2027 at least one named application-security or supply-chain-security platform (the Snyk / Endor Labs / JFrog / Protect AI / HiddenLayer class of vendors) will market a productized, named capability that scans the machine-learning data-and-metadata plane for unsafe-deserialization and untrusted-serialized-object risk — pickle/dill/joblib payloads, model checkpoints, and feature-store transformation bodies — as a first-class scanner tier, not a buried CVE-feed entry. Feast's June 24 CVE-2026-56121 is the structural trigger: a maximum-severity (CVSS 9.3 v4.0) unauthenticated RCE in which the registry server base64-decodes a user-supplied feature-view function body and hands it straight to dill.loads() before any authorization check, proving the attack surface has moved one layer below the model and inference engine into the ML plumbing that ingests serialized logic over the network. That is the same unsafe-deserialization primitive OWASP's agentic-AI work and the broader CVE drumbeat keep surfacing, and once a class of bug has both a documented exploit trail and a network-reachable, weaponizable shape, security vendors productize a dedicated detection surface for it rather than leaving it to generic dependency scanning. The falsifiable core is a NAMED, marketed product tier, module, or SKU whose stated scope explicitly covers ML serialized-artifact / deserialization / model-supply-chain scanning — announced in vendor docs, a release, or a launch. What does NOT count: a generic SCA tool merely ingesting the Feast CVE into its existing vulnerability feed, a one-off blog post or advisory, an internal research demo, or a prompt-injection / agent-runtime guardrail product (that is a different attack class). The deeper read is that zero-trust treatment of serialized ML artifacts — signing, provenance, and gated deserialization — becomes a sellable layer, but the load-bearing checkable claim is the named scanning tier.

reasoning.because: Feast CVE-2026-56121: unauthenticated CVSS-9.3 RCE; registry dill.loads() a user body pre-auth
reasoning.given: The ML attack surface dropped into the serialized data plane; the deserialization-RCE pattern recurs
reasoning.so_that: A named security vendor ships ML deserialization scanning as a marketed product tier, not a CVE-feed entry
reasoning.landing: by Q1 2027; one named vendor tier/SKU covering ML deserialization scanning
reasoning.plain_language: A critical AI-data bug let attackers run code via a booby-trapped file, so a security company will sell a scanner to catch that.

predictions.summary: Feast's June 24 CVE-2026-56121 is an unauthenticated CVSS-9.3 RCE: the registry runs dill.loads() on a user-supplied body, showing the ML attack surface dropped into the serialized data plane. Expect a named security vendor to ship ML deserialization scanning as a marketed product tier by Q1 2027.

predictions.title: AI accelerator ships confidential-inference tier with attestation by H1 2027
predictions.body: A purpose-built AI inference accelerator will ship or be unveiled with confidential computing as a named, load-bearing feature of the part itself — on-die root-of-trust, TEE-I/O so the model weights and activations stay encrypted in use across the CPU-accelerator boundary, and signed-model attestation that lets a tenant cryptographically verify which weights are running before sending data — marketed as a named confidential-inference SKU or managed tier by H1 2027. The June 24 OpenAI-Broadcom Jalapeno unveiling proved that buyer-designed rack-scale inference silicon is now real, but it disclosed no security-silicon angle, leaving an explicit gap: the inference accelerator wave so far competes on performance-per-watt and fabric bandwidth, not on confidentiality of the model and the prompt. Two structural forces close that gap. First, the same regulated and sovereign buyers driving custom-silicon economics also carry the heaviest data-residency and IP-protection requirements, and merchant accelerators already carry the primitives (NVIDIA Confidential Computing on Hopper/Blackwell, AMD SEV-SNP, Intel TDX with TEE-I/O) waiting to be productized into a named inference tier rather than a developer-preview flag. Second, the agentic-AI security cycle keeps tying risk to model-supply-chain integrity (poisoned checkpoints, unauthenticated registries), and signed-model attestation is the hardware-rooted answer to 'prove the weights I am querying are the weights I approved.' The falsifiable core is a NAMED part or managed tier where confidential inference — encrypted-in-use weights plus tenant-verifiable attestation — is the marketed feature, disclosed at a venue such as AMD Advancing AI (July 22-23), Hot Chips (August 23-25), Black Hat (August), or a hyperscaler launch. What does NOT count: a generic 'we support confidential computing' line on a GPU spec sheet with no inference-specific tier; a research paper or preprint with no shipping part; a confidential-VM offering that merely runs an unmodified accelerator without TEE-I/O or model attestation; or a restatement of an existing developer-preview that was already announced before today.

reasoning.because: Jalapeno's June 24 unveiling proved buyer-designed inference silicon is real but disclosed no security angle
reasoning.given: Regulated and sovereign inference buyers need encrypted-in-use weights and tenant-verifiable model attestation
reasoning.so_that: A vendor productizes TEE-I/O plus signed-model attestation into a named confidential-inference SKU or managed tier
reasoning.landing: Named confidential-inference accelerator tier with signed-model attestation ships by H1 2027
reasoning.plain_language: AI chips will soon offer a mode that keeps the model and your data secret and lets you check which model is really running.

predictions.summary: The June 24 Jalapeno unveiling proved buyer-designed inference silicon is real but disclosed no security angle. Because regulated and sovereign buyers need encrypted-in-use weights and verifiable model attestation, expect an AI accelerator to ship a named confidential-inference tier with TEE-I/O and signed-model attestation by H1 2027, distinct from a generic confidential-computing checkbox.
